newsitem.title: GERMANY: German opposition SPD links tax talks to coal deal.
newsitem.headline: German opposition SPD links tax talks to coal deal.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) linked on Monday their willingness to rejoin talks with the government on tax reforms to the outcome of a meeting between Chancellor Helmut Kohl and miners' leaders over coal subsidies.

The SPD pulled out of a weekend meeting called to discuss government plans for sweeping tax cuts in a gesture of solidarity with pit workers. The miners are protesting against government plans to cut aid to loss-making coal mines by more than half.
"The resumption of talks on the tax reform will depend on the government's offer," Peter Struck, the SPD's chief whip, said on the fringes of a party meeting in Berlin.

Germany's 18 pits have been at a standstill since Friday, and 3,000 miners marched on Bonn to picket the headquarters of the parties in Kohl's coalition. Thousands more demonstrated across the Ruhr and Saar coalfields.
Kohl wants to cut federal coal aid to Germany's pits to 3.8 billion marks ($2.2 billion) by 2005 from nine billion this year.

But Struck said the alternative proposed by the IG Bergbau miners union to wind down yearly subsidies to 6.5 billion marks in 2005 was "the last offer". "The government would be well-advised to take back its decision," he added.
The miners' leaders are scheduled to meet Kohl on Tuesday.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel said a cross-party compromise on taxes was still possible by Easter if the talks resumed.

But he repeated a weekend ultimatum to initiate legislation this Friday which would cut 30 billion marks in taxes if the SPD did not return to the tax talks. "The country cannot let itself to fall prey to the whims of the SPD," he told reporters in Munich.

Record post-war unemployment had driven both sides to the negotiating table to try to strike a tax deal which would avoid bitter and lengthy wrangling in parliament, where the SPD can veto tax measures through its upper house majority.
Politicians from both sides had been cosying up to each other, leading some commentators to speculate that Germany could soon see its first grand coalition since the 1960s.

But that mood has been shattered, leaving left and right trading accusations the other is holding up reforms just as Germany tries to put 4.7 million unemployed back to work and get its finances into shape for European monetary union (EMU).
"I have sympathy with the worries among miners about their jobs," Peter Hintze, general secretary of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), said in a statement.
But Hintze condemned the "irresponsible agitation" pursued by the two SPD premiers of Germany's coal mining states; North Rhine-Westphalia's Johannes Rau and Saarland's Oskar Lafontaine.

Lafontaine, who is also SPD leader, said on Sunday that tax talks could resume only if the coalition agreed to lighten the burden on ordinary families as soon as next year. He also demanded a cut in Germany's high labour overheads.

German newspapers criticised the SPD for seizing on the coal clash as the first opportunity to let the tax talks fail, even though Waigel has said he was ready to yield to some SPD demands, such as protecting tax breaks for shift workers.
"If everything is as is seems, the coalition's plans to cut coal subsidies came at just the right time for SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine," the Handelsblatt financial daily commented.

Handelsblatt added that Lafontaine had gone into the talks with serious misgivings: "He is driven by the fear that the SPD is just doing the coalition's own work and will lose out again at the general elections in 1998 as a result." ($ = 1.707 German Marks)
